etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English doom, dom, from Old English dōm (“judgement”), from Proto-West Germanic *dōm, from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰóh₁mos.

Compare West Frisian doem, Dutch doem, Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish dom, Icelandic dómur. Doublet of duma. See also deem.

quote.citation: a. 1701 (date written), John Dryden, “The First Book of Homer's Ilias”, in The Miscellaneous Works of John Dryden, […], volume IV, London:  […]  J[acob] and R[ichard] Tonson, […], published 1760, →OCLC, page 415:
quote.text: This, for the night; by day, the web and loom, / And homely houſhold-taſk, ſhall be her doom,

quote.text: "When should I expect him?" Roy said, resigned to his doom.

quote.text: "After he takes the throne, you will be arrested." / "You lie like your master, Carfax. Your doom is sealed."

definitions.definition: An undesirable fate; an impending severe occurrence or danger that seems inevitable.

quote.citation: 2004, Arthur Miller, “The Turpentine Still”, in Southwest Review, volume 89, number 4, page 479:
quote.text: unlike Vincent, he wasn't quite taken in by the outbreak of hopefulness on all sides. After all, nothing about the tanks or the process had been resolved; an air of doom still hung undisturbed over the project.

quote.citation: 2007 February, Bob Bahr, “Tapestries in Oil”, in American Artist, volume 71, number 773, page 45:
quote.text: Such paintings are inherently moody, and Elliott likes that-even as he carefully avoids dictating a specific mood. "Yesterday I painted the last light of the day-the trees looked pink, and the mountain's shadow was coming over them. It created a feeling of nostalgia... or impending doom... or still, quiet, peacefulness. It depends on the viewer's feelings about the scene, not just mine."

quote.citation: 2009 April 27, Nate Davis, “After Lions^ gamble, lots of big men tapped”, in USA Today, Sports, page 7C:
quote.text: Chung was the first of its four picks in Round 2. His arrival might spell doom for Rodney Harrison.

definitions.definition: Dread; a feeling of danger, impending danger, darkness, or despair.

quote.citation: 2006, Sophie Jordan, Once upon a wedding night:
quote.text: She halted her pacing steps as the ugly significance of Nicholas Caulfield's pending arrival washed over her. Ruin. Destitution. Doom settled like a heavy stone in her chest.

quote.citation: 2007, Terry Kay with William J. Scheick, The Year the Lights Came on, page 204:
quote.text: Feeling doom, as we learned in the beautiful folk language of blacks who knew the truth of it, began with a single unexpected oddity — a redbird out of season, hail out of cloudless skies, dogs cowering under the house

quote.citation: 2008, Beverly Fincham, Real Life Freedom, page 25:
quote.text: I'm taking medications every day; never thinking I would be spiraling into nothing but a nightmare that made me feel doom.

quote.citation: 2009 March, Deanna Roy, “Forget the rules and make the leap”, in Writer, volume 122, number 3, page 15:
quote.text: Then the smiling narrator filled me with doom: I was expected to pull my own rip cord. I nearly fainted.

quote.citation: 2010 July 20, Mark Morford, “What to do when it all goes right”, in San Francisco Chronicle:
quote.text: perhaps you do that most rare of things when reading the news: You grin, exhale, stop feeling doom in every crevasse and corner of your body.

quote.citation: 1915, Beatrice Adelaide Lees, Alfred the Great: the truth teller, maker of England, 848-899, page 211:
quote.text: "What ye will not that other men should do unto you, that do ye not unto other men." "From this one doom," comments Alfred, "a man may bethink him how he should judge every one rightly: he needs no other doombook."

quote.citation: 1600, Edward Fairfax, transl., Jerusalem Delivered, translation of Gerusalemme Liberata by Torquato Tasso:
quote.text: And there he learned of things and haps to come, / To give foreknowledge true, and certain doom.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Esdras 7:43:
quote.text: But the day of doome shall be the end of this time, and the beginning of the immortality for to come, wherein corruption is past.

quote.citation: 1861, Henry Sumner Maine, Ancient Law, page 22:
quote.text: Kings are spoken of as if they had a store of "Themistes" ready to hand for use; but it must be distinctly understood that they are not laws, but judgments, or, to take the exact Teutonic equivalent, "dooms."

quote.citation: 1915, Beatrice Adelaide Lees, Alfred the Great: the truth teller, maker of England, 848-899, page 208:
quote.text: when Alfred in turn set himself to the task of stating and interpreting the law of his kingdom, there were already precedents for him to follow, in the written "dooms" (domas) of his predecessors, — themselves but a small portion of the still unwritten custom

quote.citation: 1977, J. R. R. Tolkien, The Silmarillion, page 88:
quote.text: Therefore I say that we will go on, and this doom I add: the deeds that we shall do shall be the matter of song until the last days of Arda.

definitions.definition: (countable, obsolete) A sentence or penalty for illegal behaviour.

quote.citation: 1874, John Richard Green, A Short History of the English People:
quote.text: The first dooms of London provide especially the recovery of cattle belonging to the citizens.

quote.citation: 1828, John Erskine with Sir George Mackenzie and James Ivory, An institute of the law of Scotland, page 989:
quote.text: Appeals were by our ancient law styled falsing of dooms. They were to be entered immediately after doom or sentence was pronounced,

quote.citation: 1885, W[illiam] S[chwenck] Gilbert, Arthur Sullivan, composer, “A More Humane Mikado”, in  […]  The Mikado; or, The Town of Titipu, London: Chappel & Co., […], →OCLC, Act II, page 36:
quote.text: The billiard sharp whom anyone catches / His doom’s extremely hard— / He’s made to dwell— / In a dungeon cell / On a spot that’s always barred.

quote.citation: 1593, William Shakespeare, Titus Andronicus:
quote.text: This is the day of doom for Bassianus.

quote.citation: 2006, The H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, “Harley Got Devoured by the Undead”, in An Even Scarier Solstice:
quote.text: Harley got devoured by the undead / Lurking down in some old wizard's tomb / You can say there's no such thing as zombies / But that's how Harley Warren met his doom

quote.citation: 2009, Anne Kristin Stuart, Tangled lies:
quote.text: The engines were rumbling, missing every now and then, and Rachel leaned back in her seat, prepared to meet her doom somewhere over the Pacific. At least there was a priest at hand -- maybe she could entice him to hear a final confession.

definitions.definition: (sometimes capitalized) The Last Judgment; or, an artistic representation thereof.
(transitive) To pronounce judgment or sentence on; to condemn.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Sixth Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Absolves the just, and dooms the guilty souls.

quote.citation: 2019 April 28, Alex McLevy, “Game Of Thrones Suffers the Fog of War in the Battle against the Dead (Newbies)”, in The A.V. Club‎[1], archived from the original on 31 May 2021:
quote.text: There was certainly plenty of badass Arya before and after—more on that soon—but here was Arya the living, breathing human, outnumbered and petrified of making the one slight wrong move that would doom her.

definitions.definition: To destine; to fix irrevocably the ill fate of.

quote.citation: 1856 February, [Thomas Babington] Macaulay, “Oliver Goldsmith”, in T[homas] F[lower] E[llis], editor, The Miscellaneous Writings and Speeches of Lord Macaulay, new edition, London: Longman, Green, Reader, & Dyer, published 1871, →OCLC:
quote.text: A man of genius  […]  doomed to struggle with difficulties.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To judge; to estimate or determine as a judge.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “(please specify the page number)”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To ordain as a penalty; hence, to mulct or fine.

definitions.definition: (archaic, New England) To assess a tax upon, by estimate or at discretion.
